title: Diminutives: small words, warm tone
description: Recognise diminutives and what they add: size, warmth, politeness or irony.

blocks.text: Polish forms diminutives freely with suffixes such as -ek, -ik, -ka and -ko: dom becomes domek, kot becomes kotek, kawa becomes kawka. They can mean that something is small, but more often they add warmth, politeness or informality: a waiter may offer kawka and herbatka without implying a small cup. A second suffix intensifies the feeling: kotek, koteczek. Overused, diminutives sound childish or ironic, and they are avoided in formal writing.

blocks.translation: We have a little house by the lake.
Will you have a nice cup of coffee?
blocks.note: Kawka is friendly; the cup is not necessarily small.

blocks.translation: Our kitty is sleeping on the sofa.
The money will not earn itself.
blocks.note: Here the diminutive of pieniądze is ironic.

lines.speaker: Babcia
lines.translation: Come, darling, will you have some soup?

lines.speaker: Wnuk
lines.translation: Thank you, grandma, just a tiny bit.

lines.speaker: Babcia
lines.translation: And then a nice tea and a biscuit.

lines.speaker: Wnuk
lines.translation: Grandma, I am thirty years old!
